description: AI does the monitoring; people make the call.
summary: EmberSync brings two kinds of satellite eyes onto one fire calendar for British Columbia, Canada. NASA's MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP) see fire differently: VIIRS has finer 375 m pixels and records far more hotspots. As MODIS missions end, almost 25 years of fire history risks becoming hard to compare. We cleaned 1.79 million FIRMS detections for BC from 2001 to 2025 and fitted two factors from the 2012 to 2025 overlap years, one for hotspot counts and one for fire energy. This puts the whole record on one VIIRS scale. Our web app follows five moves: Scan the world's fire data, Spot BC's six fire centres, Block the calendar of month against year, Watch one month's map, and Make the call. Low-confidence points are kept, not dropped, and isolated detections go on a watch list with nearby place names, because all it takes is a spark. Gemini drafts a one-line insight for each fire centre and month, and people check every line before it appears. One calendar, two kinds of eyes. People make the call.
details:
What it does and how it works
EmberSync turns two satellite fire records into one calendar for British Columbia, Canada. We pulled the NASA FIRMS yearly archives for Canada: MODIS (Terra and Aqua) for 2001 to 2025, and VIIRS (Suomi NPP) for 2012 to 2025. We clipped them to BC and kept vegetation fires only, which left 1,792,662 detections. Each detection was tagged to one of BC's six fire centres and to a 0.1 degree grid cell.

MODIS sees 1 km pixels and VIIRS 375 m, so the raw counts differ. Using 1,008 fire-centre months from the overlap years, we fitted two factors by least squares: 4.92 for hotspot counts (r 0.985) and 0.515 for fire energy (r 0.988). Fire energy is fire radiative power (FRP) summed per fire centre per month. The calendar uses MODIS times the factor for 2001 to 2011, and VIIRS as observed from 2012.

The app follows five moves:

  • Scan: the world's fire data.
  • Spot: BC's six fire centres.
  • Block: a 25-year calendar of month against year.
  • Watch: one month's map.
  • Make the call: reviewed insights based on historical trends.

Benefits and intended impact
Fire managers and researchers get one consistent 25-year record, so a 2003 season can be compared fairly with a 2023 one. That continuity matters even more as MODIS winds down. Low-confidence points are kept rather than dropped. Isolated detections, the only detection in their grid cell that day, go on a watch list with the nearest named place from GeoNames, so faint early signals stay visible.


Tools

  • Python with pandas and SciPy for cleaning, the factor fit and place names.
  • React, TypeScript, Vite and D3 for the web app.
  • Google Gemini for one-line insights, drafted in batch and checked by the team before they appear.
  • NASA FIRMS data, the BC Wildfire Service fire-centre boundaries, and GeoNames.

Creativity
The five moves come from a teaching method for thinking, reading and writing. They give the app a clear path from a world view down to a single decision. The calendar makes 25 years readable at a glance, and the AI only drafts. People make the call.

Factors we considered

  • Sensor differences in pixel size and confidence scales.
  • Keeping low-confidence data rather than dropping it.
  • Not double-counting fires seen by both sensors.
  • Accuracy of the AI, so every number in an insight comes from the data.
  • A 24-hour build scope.
  • Privacy: our Gemini API key stays out of the public repo.
